lessons.title: Negotiating terms
lessons.goal: Make offers, set conditions and push back politely in a negotiation.

tip.title: Softening with the conditional
tip.body: Blunt demands (Baissez le prix !) sound aggressive in French. The conditional softens them: Seriez-vous prêts à … ? Nous pourrions … Il faudrait que … Conditions use à condition que + subjunctive (à condition que la livraison soit faite) or à condition de + infinitive when the subject is the same. Et si + imparfait (Et si nous commandions … ?) is a gentle way to float an idea. Pronunciation: in pourrions and serions, the -ions ending is one syllable for most speakers: pou-rions, se-rions — but keep the i: it's what distinguishes pourrions (would) from pourrons (will).

lessons.goal: Find common ground, make concessions and agree on a solution with a friend.

tip.title: Proposing with on and the imparfait
tip.body: Among friends, on replaces nous and makes proposals feel shared: On pourrait … Et si on + imparfait (Et si on coupait la poire en deux ?) is the classic friendly suggestion — the imparfait here has nothing to do with the past. Je veux bien means 'I'm happy to' (more willing than plain je veux). Watch the liaison in On_est d'accord and the silent final t in d'accord.

lessons.title: Asking for a pay rise
lessons.goal: Argue for a higher salary calmly and convincingly.

tip.title: Arguing with results
tip.body: In French salary talks, a well-structured argument is valued: start with facts (Depuis que je gère ce projet, …), then make a clear request with a figure in the conditional: Je souhaiterais une augmentation de huit pour cent. Rémunération sounds more formal than salaire. Pour cent: the t of cent is silent, but you hear it in liaison before a vowel (cent_euros).

lessons.title: The past conditional
lessons.goal: Talk about missed chances: J'aurais dû demander plus.

tip.title: aurais / serais + past participle
tip.body: The conditionnel passé = avoir or être in the conditional + past participle: j'aurais payé, nous serions partis. It expresses regrets and missed chances: J'aurais dû (I should have), J'aurais pu (I could have), Il aurait fallu (it would have been necessary). The past 'if' sentence is si + plus-que-parfait → conditionnel passé: Si vous aviez commandé plus tôt, vous auriez payé moins cher — never conditional after si. It also makes requests extra-polite: J'aurais voulu vous demander un service (I was hoping to ask you a favour). Pronunciation: j'aurais (conditional) ends in an open è sound, j'aurai (future) in a closed é — many speakers barely distinguish them, so context matters.

story.intro: At the flea market on the Place du Jeu de Balle in Brussels, Léa haggles with a Belgian seller over an old lamp.

culture.title: Négocier en France et au Québec
culture.body: In France, negotiation is often an intellectual exercise: people like to argue their position, may open with firm demands and enjoy some debate before conceding — and decisions often need approval from higher up. In Québec, the style tends to be more direct, informal and pragmatic, closer to North American habits: people often switch to tu quickly and aim for a gagnant-gagnant (win-win) deal, while open confrontation is usually frowned upon. Shop prices are fixed in France, Belgium, Switzerland and Canada; haggling is normal at brocantes, vide-greniers and flea markets, and expected in many West African markets.
